title: A peak element is one that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given an array where neighbors differ, return the index of any peak. Assume elements outside the array are negative infinity. Run in logarithmic time.
shortTitle: Find a Peak Element — Binary Search on the Slope

s1_definition.profdef: Finding a peak element uses binary search on the slope of the array. By comparing the middle element to its right neighbor, we learn whether we are on an ascending or descending slope and move toward the uphill direction, which is guaranteed to contain a peak. This runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space even though the array is unsorted.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank charts hourly trading volume, which rises and falls like hills. It wants any local high point, an hour busier than the hours immediately before and after. A clerk stands on the middle hour and looks at the next hour. If the next hour is busier, he walks uphill to the right because a peak must lie that way; if it is quieter, the peak is at his feet or to the left.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compare middle to its right neighbor and always walk uphill; a peak must exist in that direction.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding a peak element uses binary search on the slope of the array. By comparing the middle element to its right neighbor, we learn whether we are on an ascending or descending slope and move toward the uphill direction, which is guaranteed to contain a peak. This runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space even though the array is unsorted.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank charts hourly trading volume, which rises and falls like hills. It wants any local high point, an hour busier than the hours immediately before and after. A clerk stands on the middle hour and looks at the next hour. If the next hour is busier, he walks uphill to the right because a peak must lie that way; if it is quieter, the peak is at his feet or to the left.

**One line to remember:** Compare middle to its right neighbor and always walk uphill; a peak must exist in that direction.

sections.s2_technical:
The surprising part is that binary search works on an unsorted array here, because the problem has a slope structure we can exploit. We treat the array boundaries as negative infinity, so an ascending slope on the far right must eventually turn into a peak, and likewise on the left.

The loop is `while (low < high)` with the overflow-safe mid. We compare the middle to its immediate right neighbor. If `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, we are climbing, so a peak lies to the right, and we set `low = mid + 1`. Otherwise `arr[mid] >= arr[mid + 1]` means we are at a peak or descending, so a peak is at mid or to the left, and we set `high = mid`.

Because we always move toward the higher neighbor, and the ends are treated as negative infinity, the search is guaranteed to converge on a peak. When low equals high the loop ends and that index is a peak, so we return low.

Note that mid plus one is always valid inside the loop because the loop runs only while low is strictly less than high, which means mid is at most high minus one, so mid plus one is within bounds.

A senior-level nuance is proving termination and correctness. The invariant is that there is always a peak within the current window, because at least one boundary of the window points uphill into it. Moving toward the taller neighbor preserves this invariant while halving the window.

Another nuance is that the array need not be sorted at all, which surprises many candidates; the only requirement is that adjacent elements differ, so there is always a definite slope direction.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's trading desk records hourly trade volumes across the day, and the monitoring tool wants to flag any local peak hour, an hour busier than the hours just before and after, to investigate spikes. The volumes rise and fall unpredictably, so the array is not sorted, but we still want a fast peak finder. This is exactly the find-peak-element problem.

Problem 2 — The desk wants the peak found logarithmically so the dashboard stays responsive even with long time series, which rules out scanning every hour.

Problem 3 — Adjacent hours have differing volumes in this dataset, satisfying the no-equal-neighbors precondition that guarantees a definite slope at every step.

In the code: a `VolumeAnalyzer` holds an int array of hourly volumes. A `findPeak` method performs the slope binary search. A `PeakDemo` main finds a peak index and logs the volume there.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: volumes 120, 350, 800, 640, 200, 900, 500 (indices 0 to 6). Peaks exist at index 2 (800) and index 5 (900); we return any one.

Step 1: low 0, high 6, mid 3. arr[3] is 640, arr[4] is 200. Middle is not less than its right neighbor, so we are at a peak or descending. Move high to 3.

Step 2: low 0, high 3, mid 1. arr[1] is 350, arr[2] is 800. Middle is less than its right neighbor, so we are climbing. Move low to 2.

Step 3: low 2, high 3, mid 2. arr[2] is 800, arr[3] is 640. Middle is not less than its right neighbor, so move high to 2.

Step 4: low 2 equals high 2, loop ends. Return index 2, where volume 800 is greater than both neighbors 350 and 640. It is a valid peak.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 22:35:00 [INFO] Found a local peak hour
2026-10-26 22:35:00 [INFO] Peak at hour index 2 with volume 800
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [120 350 800 640 200 900 500]  (hills)
    │
    ▼ compare mid vs mid+1 → walk uphill
  low0 high6 mid3: 640 >= 200 → high=3
  low0 high3 mid1: 350 < 800  → low=2
  low2 high3 mid2: 800 >= 640 → high=2
  low==high==2
    │
    ▼
  Output: index 2 (volume 800 > neighbors 350 and 640)
```

```
  2.   loop while low<high: climbing? low=mid+1 : high=mid
  3.   return low
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding a peak element is a surprising case where binary search works on an array that is not sorted at all, because the problem has a slope structure I can exploit. On each step I compare the middle element to its immediate right neighbor. If the right neighbor is larger, I am climbing a slope, and since the array boundaries behave like negative infinity, that uphill direction must eventually turn into a peak, so I move low to the right of the middle. If the right neighbor is smaller or equal, then the middle is itself a peak or a peak lies to its left, so I move high down to the middle, keeping the middle as a candidate.

Because I always walk toward the taller neighbor, the invariant that a peak exists somewhere inside the current window is preserved while the window halves each step, so the search converges on a peak in logarithmic time. The index mid plus one is always safe to read because the loop only runs while low is strictly less than high, which keeps the middle at least one step short of the right edge.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, the trading desk records hourly trade volumes across the day, and the monitoring dashboard flags local peak hours, hours busier than the ones immediately before and after, to investigate spikes. The volumes rise and fall unpredictably so the series is unsorted, yet this slope-based binary search finds a peak logarithmically, keeping the dashboard responsive even over long time series.

The insight I emphasize in interviews is the proof of correctness: there is always a peak within the window because at least one boundary points uphill into it, and moving toward the higher neighbor never destroys that guarantee. That is why the method is correct, and being able to articulate the invariant rather than just reciting the code is what demonstrates real understanding.
